title: Bidirectional BFS: Meet-in-the-Middle Magic!
description: Watch how Bidirectional BFS searches from start and goal simultaneously on real street-grid graphs. The two frontiers expand until they meet, often reducing explored nodes dramatically versus single-source BFS.
ig_caption:
🧭✨ Richmond District streets, but make them a graph. In this visualization, **Bidirectional BFS** runs two BFS waves—one from the start node and one from the target—until the frontiers **intersect**. 

🔍 Why it’s powerful (graph theory time): on an unweighted graph like a street network, BFS guarantees shortest paths, but doing it from both ends shrinks the search space from ~**O(b^d)** down toward ~**O(b^(d/2))** in many practical cases (b = branching factor, d = path length). 

🗺️ Imagine each intersection as a vertex and each road segment as an edge. Instead of expanding outward blindly, we’re effectively performing a **meet-in-the-middle** shortest-path strategy—frontiers “handshake” where the route becomes inevitable. 

👉 Want the next city-route visual? Drop a 🧠 in the comments and tell me: should we weight roads by travel time (Dijkstra/A*) next?
fb_caption:
Ever wonder how computers find the fastest route across a city map? In this reel, **Bidirectional BFS** builds two BFS trees on the street graph—one expanding from the start and one from the goal—then stops as soon as the paths meet, producing the shortest route on an unweighted graph. 

📍Graph search meets real-world streets—share this with a friend who loves algorithms, and comment which district you want next!
yt_description:
Bidirectional BFS visualization on a real street map (Richmond District, San Francisco)! 🚦 This video shows how two BFS searches expand from start and destination simultaneously, meeting in the middle to find shortest paths on unweighted graphs. 

Keywords: Bidirectional BFS, shortest path, graph search, BFS visualization, coding algorithms, computer science, data structures, real map pathfinding.

Mechanics: Start frontier + Goal frontier → expand level-by-level → intersection found → reconstruct shortest path. Like, subscribe, and comment the next city for the visualization!
